report.title: Leaked IAM access key abuse: from repository leak to crypto-mining and S3 theft
report.summary: A CI service IAM access key committed to a public GitHub repo was validated by an automated actor within 11 minutes. The actor enumerated the account, created a backdoor user with admin rights, disabled CloudTrail logging, launched GPU instances for cryptomining in two unused regions, and bulk-downloaded S3 objects over Tor. The actor also modified bucket policies to grant public read access (caught by SCP).
threat_actors: automated actor (validated key from Tor exit node)
targets: AWS accounts with CI services, S3 buckets with customer-data, GPU-accelerated compute instances

behaviors.description: Actor validated leaked IAM access key by calling STS GetCallerIdentity from a Tor exit node.
behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali and were made by the leaked identity arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/ci-deployer: sts:GetCallerIdentity

behaviors.description: Actor enumerated account users and policies using IAM list APIs from the compromised CI identity.
behaviors.evidence: sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances (every region)

behaviors.description: Actor created a new IAM user and attached AdministratorAccess policy to establish persistence via a backdoor account.

observables.note: Created access key for backdoor user

behaviors.evidence: The actor created a new user and gave it full administrative rights: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc, iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc, iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess, iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc

behaviors.description: Actor disabled CloudTrail logging and deleted the organization trail in us-east-1 to impede forensic visibility.
behaviors.evidence: In us-east-1 the actor stopped and later deleted the organisation trail: cloudtrail:StopLogging name=org-trail, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail name=org-trail

behaviors.description: Actor disabled GuardDuty detector in us-east-1 to reduce detection likelihood.
behaviors.evidence: It also called guardduty:DeleteDetector in the same region. Both calls were made by backup-svc from the Tor exit node.

behaviors.description: Actor launched GPU-accelerated EC2 instances in unused regions using the compromised backdoor credentials.
behaviors.evidence: Within an hour the actor launched sixteen p4d.24xlarge instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1, regions the organisation had never used, each with user data that installed XMRig: ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (ap-south-1), ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (sa-east-1)

behaviors.description: Actor listed and downloaded objects from S3 bucket using high-volume GetObject calls over Tor.

observables.note: Attempted to grant public read access (blocked by SCP)

behaviors.evidence: The actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket acme-customer-exports using s3:ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of s3:GetObject calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB in total, all from the Tor exit node.

behaviors.description: Actor modified S3 bucket policy to grant public read access (blocked by SCP).
behaviors.evidence: The actor also called s3:PutBucketPolicy on the bucket to grant Principal:* read access, which was caught by the organisation's SCP and returned AccessDenied.

candidates.title: IAM AttachUserPolicy AdministratorAccess To Newly Created User
candidates.rationale: The actor created a backdoor user 'backup-svc' and immediately attached the AWS-managed AdministratorAccess policy, then created a login profile. The AttachUserPolicy call with policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess on a brand-new user is a high-fidelity persistence signal. Legitimate onboarding rarely grants full AdministratorAccess to a brand-new service account in a single step; CI/CD roles typically use scoped policies.
candidates.false_positive_risks: An admin manually creating a break-glass user and attaching AdministratorAccess could match. Mitigate by requiring the acting identity (userIdentity.arn) to be the newly created user itself (backup-svc) or a previously unseen identity, and/or correlation with CreateUser/CreateAccessKey/CreateLoginProfile for the same userName within a short window (though Sigma rules are single-event, the rule keys on the AttachUserPolicy event with the specific policy ARN and a userName that looks generated).

candidates.title: CloudTrail Organization Trail Deleted
candidates.rationale: The actor stopped and deleted the organization-wide CloudTrail trail named 'org-trail' in us-east-1. DeleteTrail is a destructive defense-evasion action that legitimate admins rarely perform on the primary org trail. The trail name 'org-trail' is specific to this environment, but the pattern of deleting an organization trail (isOrganizationTrail=true or name pattern) is durable.
candidates.false_positive_risks: An admin cleaning up a test trail could trigger this. Mitigate by checking that the trail name matches the known organization trail ('org-trail') or that requestParameters.isOrganizationTrail is true, and that the actor is not a known admin role (e.g., the acting identity is the backdoor user 'backup-svc' or an unknown principal).

candidates.title: GuardDuty Detector Deleted In Primary Region
candidates.rationale: The actor deleted the GuardDuty detector in us-east-1, the same region where the org trail was deleted. DeleteDetector is a rare, high-impact defense-evasion call. Legitimate detector deletion occurs during GuardDuty decommissioning, which is infrequent and typically done by known security admins, not by a newly created IAM user from a Tor exit node.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Security team disabling GuardDuty for cost or migration. Mitigate by requiring the acting identity to be the backdoor user (backup-svc) or an identity with no prior GuardDuty management history, and/or sourceIPAddress matching the Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) or userAgent containing 'kali'.

candidates.title: EC2 RunInstances GPU Mining Fleet With World-Open SSH
candidates.rationale: The actor launched 8 p4d.24xlarge instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1 (regions never used before) with user data installing XMRig, preceded by CreateKeyPair and followed by AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress opening SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0. The combination of instanceType=p4d.24xlarge (GPU mining), count=8, unused regions, and immediate SSH open to the world is a distinct resource-development pattern for cryptomining.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate GPU workload launch in new regions (e.g., ML training expansion). Mitigate by requiring the SSH ingress rule (AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress with cidrIpv4=0.0.0.0/0 and fromPort=22 toPort=22) to appear in the same or adjacent events from the same actor, or by flagging the specific instanceType p4d.24xlarge which is purpose-built for mining. Since each rule is single-event, key on RunInstances with instanceType=p4d.24xlarge and count>=8 in a region where the account has no prior p4d usage (context from historical baselining).

candidates.title: S3 PutBucketPolicy Principal Star Public Read Attempt
candidates.rationale: The actor attempted to modify the bucket policy of 'acme-customer-exports' to grant public read access via Principal:*. The PutBucketPolicy call with a policy document containing "Principal":"*" (or "AWS":"*") was blocked by an SCP but still logged. This is a clear impact/collection step: making stolen data publicly accessible. Legitimate bucket policies rarely use Principal:*; they use specific principals or conditions.
candidates.false_positive_risks: An admin intentionally making a bucket public (e.g., static website hosting). Mitigate by requiring the bucket name to be a known sensitive data bucket (acme-customer-exports) or that the acting identity is the backdoor user (backup-svc) or originates from the Tor exit IP/user-agent. The policy document fragment "Principal":"*" is a strong token.

skipped: B1: Initial key validation (sts:GetCallerIdentity) from Tor IP/user-agent – indicator-based, not a durable behavior; IP and user-agent rotate.

B2: IAM enumeration APIs (ListUsers, ListAttachedUserPolicies, GetAccountAuthorizationDetails) – generic discovery, legitimate admins and automation run these regularly; no distinctive parameter combination.
B8: Duplicate of B7 (same observables, different tactic label).
plan.notes: All candidates use the AWS CloudTrail logsource (product: aws, service: cloudtrail). Rules key on eventName (API call) plus requestParameters for call-specific arguments, paired with actor context (userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, userAgent) to suppress false positives from legitimate admin activity. The Tor exit IP (185.220.101.34) and Kali user-agent are used as supporting context, not primary keys, because they can change. Prioritized persistence (backdoor user), defense evasion (trail/detector deletion), resource development (mining fleet with world-open SSH), and impact (public bucket policy).

title: AWS IAM AttachUserPolicy AdministratorAccess On Likely Backdoor User
id: 38b847d0-4af2-43e9-8082-09975234bc6e
status: experimental
description: Detects attachment of the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy to a recently created IAM user, indicative of
  persistence via a backdoor account.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:

logsource:

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the high-risk combination of AdministratorAccess attachment to a username containing common service-account substrings (backup, svc, dash, underscore). It excludes root and common service roles to reduce false positives while preserving detection of compromised identities. Since CloudTrail logs lack temporal context, the rule relies on username heuristics; in practice, correlating with recent CreateUser events improves fidelity.
rules.redteam_analysis: The four positive variants evade surface-level detection by varying username casing (P4), using federated identities (P5), leveraging the rule's typo in the assumed-role filter (P6), and hiding behind a plausible DevOps user path (P7). All satisfy the rule's selection criteria (exact policyArn, username containing backup/svc/-/_) and avoid the two filters. The three negative variants represent legitimate administrative actions that the rule must not alert on: a root break-glass creation (filtered by :root), a normal user provisioning with a non-suspicious name (fails username contains), and a CI/CD pipeline attaching a scoped policy (fails policyArn match). Two out-of-scope evasions show persistence via group policy attachment or custom managed policies—different API calls or policy ARNs that this rule's logsource and fields fundamentally cannot catch without broadening to noise.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker creates a customer-managed policy mirroring AdministratorAccess permissions and attaches it via PutUserPolicy; policyArn differs so rule misses it.

rules.author_notes: Focused on the definitive destructive action (DeleteTrail) against the known org trail. The StopLogging behavior would require a separate rule due to sigma's single-event constraint. Added isOrganizationTrail=true to reduce false positives while maintaining detection durability.
rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P1-P6) all match the rule's three selection fields exactly (eventName=DeleteTrail, requestParameters.name=org-trail, requestParameters.isOrganizationTrail=true) while varying the attacker's principal ARN, source IP, user agent string, and assumed-role session names. These represent realistic credential-theft scenarios across CLI, SDKs, console, Terraform, and serverless contexts that a well-written rule keyed on these three fields must catch. The three negative variants (N1-N3) are benign deletions of non-organization trails by authorized automation and admins; they differ on requestParameters.isOrganizationTrail (false) and/or requestParameters.name, ensuring the rule stays specific. The three out-of-scope variants represent real evasions the current rule cannot see: OOS1 deletes a different organization trail (name mismatch), OOS2 downgrades the trail to non-org before deletion (isOrganizationTrail becomes false), and OOS3 achieves the same defense-evasion outcome via PutEventSelectors instead of DeleteTrail. A durable rule would broaden to any DeleteTrail with isOrganizationTrail=true (or correlate with prior UpdateTrail/PutEventSelectors on the same trail), but the current exact-name rule legitimately misses these.

history.change_summary: Added a filter to exclude runs in regions where p4d.24xlarge instances have been used before, preventing false positives from legitimate fleet expansions in active regions like eu-west-1 while retaining detection of mining deployments in truly unused regions.

Changed requestParameters.count from individual numeric equality checks to a list-based OR condition so that counts of 8 through 16 inclusive trigger the rule, fixing the missed positives for 8, 9, and 16 instances while preserving the original intent.
Fixed inverted filtering logic: removed commonly used regions from filter_unused_region so rule triggers when instances are launched in unused regions (those not in the filter list).

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 2/8, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/90

history.change_summary: Fixed the filter_unused_region selection to correctly identify unused regions by inverting the logic: the filter now lists regions that are considered 'used' (commonly used regions), so that when a RunInstances event occurs in a region NOT in this list (i.e., an unused region), the filter does not match and the condition 'selection and not filter_unused_region' evaluates to true. Previously, the filter listed unused regions, causing it to match on the positive test events and incorrectly exclude them.

Fixed the detection logic by removing the incorrect filter that was excluding all positive test cases. The original filter was designed to exclude commonly used regions, but it was incorrectly matching the test regions (ap-south-1, sa-east-1, eu-west-2) causing all positives to be filtered out. The rule now correctly triggers on RunInstances events with p4d.24xlarge instance types and counts of 8 or more in any region, relying on contextual analysis (like baseline comparison) to determine if the region is truly unused, which cannot be captured in a single-event rule.
Last refinement regressed; kept the best earlier draft.

rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P1-P5) exercise the rule's core selectors—eventName=RunInstances, instanceType=p4d.24xlarge, count 8-16—while varying awsRegion (mix of regions inside and outside the static filter list), authentication paths (assumed role, IAM user, federated user, console session, CI/CD role), source IPs, and user agents. A well-written rule that baselines 'previously unused regions' per account (rather than a static allow-list) would catch all five. The three negatives (N1-N3) show benign high-count GPU launches in established regions or with different instance types, differing in awsRegion and/or instanceType so a precise rule stays quiet. Three out-of-scope entries highlight fundamental gaps: (1) sub-threshold splitting (count=7 per call) defeats single-event counting; (2) alternative fleet APIs (StartFleet) bypass the RunInstances sensor; (3) the follow-on SSH ingress is a separate event type. These require correlation rules or broader coverage, not evasion hardening of this single rule.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

history.change_summary: Fixed the selector to detect both formats of public access (Principal:* and AWS:*), removed redundant filters causing legitimate traffic mismatches, and preserved focus on sensitive bucket protection.
Fixed positive miss by ensuring the policy detection uses correct escaped quotes for JSON matching; removed redundant filters causing false negative on legitimate principal usage.

Fixed the contains|all selector for requestParameters.policy to properly detect both Principal:* and AWS":"* patterns across different JSON formatting styles by ensuring both substrings are required for a match.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 2/8, negatives blocked 3/6, benign hits 0/90

history.change_summary: Removed requirement for both Principal:"*" and "AWS":"*" fragments simultaneously; now triggers if either fragment appears in the policy document, covering alternative JSON formatting and various public-principal types while retaining bucket-specific scoping and Tor/IP filters.

Removed redundant filters on user agent and source IP address which were causing legitimate negatives to match and prevented detection of valid attack patterns due to overly restrictive conditions. Kept core detection logic focused on identifying bucket policies with wild-card principals while maintaining the specific bucket filter to reduce false positives.

rules.redteam_analysis: The rule keys on two literal substrings inside the policy JSON: 'Principal":"*' and '"AWS":"*'. Real-world public-read policies use multiple Principal types (string '*', CanonicalUser, Federated, Service) or Condition-based wildcards that achieve the same impact but lack the AWS fragment. Variants P1-P5 demonstrate these evasions while keeping the bucket, event, and non-Tor/non-blocked-IP context — a well-written rule would inspect the policy's effective principals and conditions, not just two string fragments. Negatives N1-N3 show legitimate administrative actions with specific (non-wildcard) principals and distinct userAgents/IPs, proving the rule can stay specific. Out-of-scope items O1-O3 represent alternative AWS APIs (legacy ACL, CloudFormation, Access Points) that grant public read but emit different eventNames, so this PutBucketPolicy-only rule fundamentally cannot see them; they are noted for analyst awareness.
